_comment: Hook registration for the pi coding agent (@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent).
pi has no built-in hooks.json mechanism — it has a TypeScript extension API — so the
bridge extension in pi/extensions/polyforge/ READS this file and subscribes to the
listed pi events, converting each into the Claude Code-shaped JSON the hook scripts
already parse on stdin. The hook scripts themselves are unchanged and shared with the
other three runtimes.
The matchers live here, in data, rather than inline in the extension, for one reason:
tests/pf-commit-guard.test.sh asserts that every runtime's registration file routes
pf_commit/pr/wrap/ship to pf-commit-guard and does NOT route unrelated tools. A matcher
hardcoded in TypeScript would be invisible to that gate.
'event' keys are pi's own event names (ExtensionAPI.on overloads in
core/extensions/types.d.ts). 'match' declares WHICH SUBJECT the matcher is applied to,
and each event offers exactly one:
toolName -> event.toolName          (tool_call, tool_result)
text     -> event.text              (input)
always   -> no matching, always run (session_start)
An entry whose 'match' disagrees with the event it is filed under is SKIPPED, not
silently tested against the wrong string — e.g. match:"text" under tool_call would
otherwise become a rule that never fires and never complains. Omitting 'match' means
"whatever this event offers". Where a matcher has a capturing group (the input entry),
the FIRST group is the value handed to the script.

_why: IR1 bypass doors, denied unconditionally. Both tools take the REAL tool name in a
parameter (mcpScript in a JS snippet, mcp in `tool`), so a gate keyed on tool name
sees only `mcp`/`mcpScript` and the pf_commit underneath goes unguarded.
settings.scriptMode:false and settings.disableProxyTool:true in .mcp.json are the
first line and are asserted by tests/pi-runtime.test.sh. They are NOT sufficient:
measured on pi-mcp-adapter 2.32.1, the proxy tool is registered when ANY of three
conditions holds (index.ts:1192) --
config.settings?.disableProxyTool !== true
|| directSpecs.length === 0
|| missingConfiguredDirectToolServers.length > 0
-- so on a COLD metadata cache (~/.pi/agent/mcp-cache.json absent, i.e. the very
first session after install) `mcp` is registered despite the key being true. Two-arm
measurement, identical config, cache the only variable: cold => 55 tools with `mcp`,
warm => 54 without. The same third condition re-opens it whenever MCP_DIRECT_TOOLS
narrows the direct-tool set, which no config-file check can see.
This entry closes that window in our own code rather than depending on third-party
behaviour. It has no `bash`: the deny is issued directly by the bridge.
tool_call.deny: [polyforge IR1] BLOCKED: the `mcp` proxy and `mcpScript` tools carry the real MCP tool name inside their arguments, so a write to git could reach pf_commit/pf_pr/pf_wrap/pf_ship without passing the polyforge commit guard. Call the polyforge_pf_* tool directly instead — all 45 are registered individually.

_why: The emitted tool name is not fixed by the server name alone — pi-mcp-adapter's
resolveToolPrefix is `definition?.toolPrefix ?? globalPrefix ?? "server"`, and the
three non-default values change the spelling out from under a name-keyed gate:
server (default) -> polyforge_pf_commit
none             -> pf_commit
mcp              -> mcp__polyforge_pf_commit
toolPrefix is settable globally AND per-server, so pinning it in mcp.json is not
enough on its own. This matcher therefore accepts all three spellings, and
tests/pi-runtime.test.sh asserts the pinned value as well — either alone leaves a
one-key edit that silently turns IR1 off. pf-commit-guard itself already copes:
rsplit("__") plus the polyforge_ strip reduce every one of them to pf_commit.
